# TAG Team Reflection - WC 19/10/2026

### Before Wednesday’s team meeting (up to 21/10/2026)

I carried out EDA on my three assigned files (`hourlySteps_merged`, `heartrate_seconds_merged`, `weightLogInfo_merged`). What stood out most was how many athletes appear in each dataset. Every athlete was present in the hourly steps data, but only 8 appeared in the weight data.

The gap in coverage matters because of how the data is likely to be collected. Steps are recorded automatically by the FitBit device, which explains the full coverage. Weight is probably entered manually, so fewer athletes use it. This may be down to a reluctance to share it. Manual entry also makes the data less reliable, because it depends on athletes entering accurate values consistently. These are my interpretations of the pattern, not confirmed facts.

This has direct design consequences. A weight page built on 8 athletes cannot be treated like the activity page, which has full coverage. Comparisons or leader boards based on weight could be misleading, so the dashboard should show how many athletes the data covers and handle missing data clearly. This created a challenge for deciding how to present weight information on the dashboard because this would affect how the page is designed and tested. To help decide this, I took it to the team as a question for the wireframe discussion. This showed me that a good dashboard has to account for the quality and coverage of the data behind each page, not only what the data can show. Basing my requirements on the EDA, rather than assumptions, meant they already reflected these limits, and I arrived at the meeting on Wednesday with something to contribute.

### **TAG Team Meeting (Microsoft Teams) - 21/10/2026**

At the 30 minute team meeting we discussed the EDA each of us had completed and agreed what needed doing by Friday. I created a shared Word Document, linked to the project overview markdown, to record all the requirements. Once we had agreed next steps, I took the lead on dividing tasks so we could submit on time. Hanifah took on the 500-word EDA report, drawing on everyone's individual EDA. She also asked each of us to contribute 5-8 requirements and to propose visualisations using ggplot or plotly.

The initials system gave clear ownership and made everyone's contribution visible. It also avoided duplicated requirements. Dividing the tasks early meant everyone left knowing what they had to do and by when, which supported meeting the deadline. Hanifah's minimum requirements target raised accountability across the team. This meeting also set up Friday's call, because roles and a shared document were agreed in advance.

### Between Wednesday and Friday

I created the initial R Shiny dashboard, with a sidebar navigating to five pages: activity, sleep, calories, weight, and heart rate. I used a modular approach and decided on the project structure:

``` text
2007_tag_task_1/
├── app.R # loads packages, sources R/ files, defines UI and server
└── R/
    ├── functions/              # Reusable helpers shared across pages
    │   ├── kpi_widget.R        # KPI widget
    │   └── leaderboard_dt.R    # Leaderboard DT rendering
    ├── global/                 # Contains Data loading functions 
    └── pages/                  # One module per dashboard page
        ├── activity.R
        ├── sleep.R
        ├── calories.R
        ├── weight.R
        └── heart_rate.R
```

I also initiated the wireframe. While building, I identified areas where a general function could be reused instead of repeating code, such as KIP widgets and the leader board DataTable (DT) rendering. I took responsibility for dividing the written requirements into each specific page.

The modular structure puts each page in its own file, so team members can work on different pages without merge conflicts, and the code is easier to test and maintain. Identifying reusable functions early avoids duplicated code and keeps the dashboard visually consistent. Splitting the requirements by page makes testing easier, because each page can be checked against its own requirements. It also makes it clearer who does what. Starting the wireframe gave the team something to react to on Friday instead of a blank page.

### **TAG Team Meeting (Microsoft Teams) - 23/10/2026**

As a team we worked together on the wireframe in a 30 minute call and discussed which plots to use on each page. Some of these came from the EDA we had been doing for the past week. We also scheduled a meeting for 28/10/2026, which is the project deadline, to record the 6 minute retrospective video explaining how the dashboard works. With 6 teams members including me, each of us will present one minute.

Basing the plots on our EDA means the design is driven by what the data shows. Working collaboratively meant everyone had input, which should increase ownership of the final dashboard. This call built on Wednesday's meeting, where roles and a shared requirements document were already agreed. That let us spend time on the design decisions instead of sorting out who was doing what.

Scheduling the video meeting now was important because it fixes a clear deadline. A one minute slot each divides the work evenly and means everyone has to understand and explain their own part of the dashboard. The risk is that 6 separate minutes can feel disjointed in the video demonstration, so we will need to agree on the order and a consistent structure so the video flows.

Communication has not been a difficulty within the team, as every member has attended all meetings so far, which has made it easy to share ideas and make decisions quickly. The harder part was deciding on the overall design of the dashboard, specifically whether it should be a single page or multi page dashboard. The required long discussion, as each of us had a different view of the best approach, and we had to weigh up the pros and cons of each. A single page would show everything at once and be simpler to navigate, but could become cluttered with five different categories. A multi page approach gives us each topic its own space and suits dividing the work between team members, but risks making it harder to compare data across topics. We settled on a multi page dashboard with sidebar navigation because this gives clearer page ownership and room for plots and different filtering functionalities tailored to each category. This showed me that design decisions in a team can take longer than technical ones, because the design depends on peoples priorities that can vary rather than one right answer. Hearing everyone reasoning rather than going with the first idea led to a decision that the whole team could support. Next time, I would suggest design conversations have a structured criteria to them next time so we can compare options more efficiently.

### Next Steps

By the end of Monday I would have written the reusable function for the KIP widgets, so everyone can use them when developing their pages. I will also establish the page-by-page breakdown of requirements, so everyone knows which page and requirements they own. I will also begin working on `mod_heartrate.R` establishing the UI and Server functionality as well as finalising wireframe details for this part of the dashboard.

As a team we will then use the finalised wireframe to guide development, and check each page against its requirements as it is built. We will keep the shared requirements document up to date as things change and review progress at the next team meeting on 26/10/2026.

I will continue to develop my leadership and delegation by checking in with other members in the team on blockers before deadlines, rather than only at meetings. As well as this, I will perform an outstanding work for reviewing other team members code promptly so work can be merged back and progress can be made.
